definitions.type: spatial Laplace operator applied componentwise to u
definitions.definition: For x in R^n and t>0, Δ_xu(x,t)=sum_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t), component by component. The notation u_t,u_tt,∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t denotes the corresponding classical partial derivatives on R^n×(0,∞). D_xu is the m-by-n matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and |D_xu|^2 is its Frobenius square sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|^2. Vectors have the Euclidean dot product and norm. Spatial integrals are Lebesgue integrals on R^n; boxes carry the restricted Lebesgue measure. int denotes topological interior and 1_A denotes the indicator of a set A.
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+sum_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2, for x in R^n and t>0, with exactly the Euclidean and Frobenius normalization of problem.md:38-46.

inputs.statement: n and m are integers with n≥1 and m≥1.

For every t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊂R^n and R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and r∈J. Put Q=[-R,R]^n; its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞. Every positive-order partial derivative of u is zero on (R^n\C)×int J. For each r∈int J the following scalar spatial functions are continuous, bounded on Q, zero outside C, and Lebesgue integrable on R^n: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t·u_tt, u_t·∂_{x_j}u, ∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), for each 1≤j≤n. Consequently e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable for every t>0.

output.statement: For every t>0 and every spatial index 1≤j≤n, the scalar functions ∂_{x_j}u(·,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(·,t) and u_t(·,t)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(·,t) are Lebesgue integrable on R^n, and ∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫_{R^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, with all terms evaluated at time t.

locals.declaration: Choose compact C from N002 at t0.
Together with C choose R>0 from N002 at t0.
Let Phi(y,s) be the point of R^n with j-th coordinate s and its other n-1 coordinates given by y in increasing coordinate order.
Fix an arbitrary vector y of the n-1 coordinates other than j.
For the fixed y, define phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)).
Let Qother=[-R,R]^(n-1) in the remaining-coordinate space.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and a spatial index j∈{1,...,n}. H001 gives n≥1, so the remaining-coordinate space has dimension n-1≥0. Set J=[t0/2,3t0/2], choose C and R>0 from N002, and put Q=[-R,R]^n. Since t0∈int J, N002 gives integrability of the derivative products in the exported conclusion and of ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u), all zero outside C. Also C⊂int Q and Q has finite measure.

produces.statement: At time t0 the functions ∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) are integrable on R^n and zero outside C; C⊂int Q, with C compact and Q=[-R,R]^n of finite measure.

argument.text: Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). By H002 it is smooth in x, and the product rule gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. It is zero off C by N002. As C is closed and contained in int Q, g is identically zero on the open complement of C, which contains the boundary of Q. Hence g vanishes on a neighborhood of that boundary. Define the coordinate insertion map Phi(y,s) by placing s in coordinate j and the vector y in the remaining coordinates, in increasing coordinate order.

produces.statement: g is smooth on R^n, zero on R^n\C, and ∂_{x_j}g(x)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) for every x∈R^n. In particular g is zero near the boundary of Q.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary y∈R^(n-1) and define phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)) for s∈R. F002 and the chain rule give the derivative phi'(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)) at every real s, including ±R. This derivative is continuous and hence bounded and Lebesgue interval-integrable on [-R,R]. Apply M003 with V=R, endpoints -R,R, f=phi, and derivative d(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)). The integral equals phi(R)-phi(-R). Each endpoint has j-th coordinate ±R and is outside C⊂(-R,R)^n, so both values are zero by F002. Therefore ∫_{-R}^R ∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s))ds=0. Quantify over the arbitrary y. The oriented interval integral is the usual restricted Lebesgue integral here since -R<R, and including or deleting the singleton endpoints does not affect a Lebesgue integral.

Let Qother=[-R,R]^(n-1) and w(y,s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)). Splitting off coordinate j identifies Q with Qother×[-R,R]. Under Phi, Lebesgue measure on R^n is the product of Lebesgue measures on the remaining coordinates and on R: on every coordinate rectangle the image has exactly the product of the side lengths, and these rectangles generate the Borel sigma algebra; uniqueness of sigma-finite measures gives the identification, also for the completed Lebesgue integrals of the continuous functions used here. If n=1, the remaining-coordinate space is R^0, a singleton of measure 1, so the same statement holds. On the compact product box, w is continuous and bounded by F002, hence measurable and absolutely integrable. Its two summands from F002 have the same property, in agreement with F001. Apply M002 with X=R^(n-1), Y=R, V=R, the Lebesgue measures restricted to Qother and [-R,R], and f=w. These measures are finite, thus s-finite. The result and F003 yield ∫_Q∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{Qother}(∫_{[-R,R]}w(y,s)ds)dy=∫_{Qother}0dy=0.

By F001 the derivative and both summands in F002 are zero outside Q, so their Q-integrals equal their R^n-integrals. Integrate the product rule F002, use F004 and linearity for the integrable summands from F001: 0=∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{R^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, all at time t0. Symmetry of the dot product and rearrangement prove ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. The asserted integrability is part of F001. Since t0 and j were arbitrary this proves the exported conclusion.

applications.bindings: Set V=R, a=-R, b=R, f(s)=phi(s)=g(Phi(y,s)), d(s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)), at the current arbitrary remaining-coordinate vector y.
hypothesis_checks: R with its usual norm is a complete normed additive commutative group and real normed vector space.
F002 gives smooth g; the coordinate insertion map is affine with velocity the j-th coordinate vector, so the chain rule gives derivative d(s) at every s, in particular throughout [-R,R].
The same smoothness makes d continuous; on the compact interval [-R,R] it is bounded and measurable, giving finite absolute integral and interval integrability.

applications.bindings: Set X=R^(n-1) (remaining coordinates), Y=R (coordinate j), V=R, mu=Lebesgue measure restricted to Qother, nu=Lebesgue measure restricted to [-R,R], and f(y,s)=w(y,s)=∂_{x_j}g(Phi(y,s)).
hypothesis_checks: The spaces have their usual measurable structures, the two restricted Lebesgue measures are measures, and R has its standard real normed vector space structure. The coordinate/product measure identification is established in S004 using rectangle volumes and sigma-finite uniqueness.
Both restricted box measures are finite (including the dimension-zero singleton of measure 1 when n=1), hence s-finite.
F002 makes w continuous. It is bounded on compact Qother×[-R,R], and the product measure is finite, so its norm has finite integral; this proves product integrability before applying M002.
